content: In multiple clinical trials, random sequence generation was employed; however, neither caregivers nor investigators were blinded in any of these studies. In one specific trial conducted in Darmstadt in 2005, there was a disruption in the randomization process, which may have led to an unequal distribution of infants between the study groups. The findings compared CPAP to supplemental oxygen, showing a reduction of 187 cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 259 fewer to 93 fewer cases). The certainty of evidence was assessed, considering risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Another Cochrane review by Ho JJ, Subramaniam P, Sivakaanthan A, and Davis PG in 2020 compared early versus delayed initiation of CPAP in preterm infants with respiratory distress. The results indicated an increase of 25 cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 53 fewer to 1,000 more cases). Certainty of evidence was evaluated, with considerations for bias and imprecision. A 2021 Cochrane review by Subramaniam P, Ho JJ, and Davis PG examined the prophylactic or very early initiation of CPAP in preterm infants. When comparing immediate CPAP to supplemental oxygen, there were 30 fewer cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 61 fewer to 17 more cases). When comparing immediate CPAP to mechanical ventilation, there were 42 fewer cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 76 fewer to 4 fewer cases). Certainty of evidence was assessed, with attention to bias and imprecision. The findings showed 62 more cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 18 more to 135 more cases). Certainty of evidence was evaluated, considering risks of bias and imprecision. Another 2022 Cochrane review by Marques K, Roehr CC, Bruschettini M, Davis PG, and Soll R focused on the use of methylxanthines for preventing and treating apnea in preterm infants. Compared to placebo or no treatment, methylxanthines resulted in 79 fewer cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 105 fewer to 4 fewer cases). Certainty of evidence was assessed, with considerations for bias and imprecision. A systematic review and meta-analysis by North K, Whelan R, Folger LV, Lawford H, Olson I, and Driker S in 2022 examined family involvement in the routine care of hospitalized preterm or low birth weight infants. The findings showed 7 fewer cases per 1,000 infants (ranging from 19 fewer to 15 more cases). Certainty of evidence was evaluated, considering risks of bias and imprecision. Another systematic review and meta-analysis by Bedwell C, Lavender T, Tate N, and Danna VA explored interventions to support parents, families, and caregivers in caring for premature or low birth weight infants at home. Comparisons included education and counseling versus usual care, peer support versus usual care, discharge preparation versus usual care, and digital information systems versus usual care. The findings varied across outcomes, with certainty of evidence assessed for each comparison, considering risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Lastly, home visits to support families in providing care for premature or low birth weight infants were compared to usual care. The findings indicated improvements in some outcomes, with certainty of evidence evaluated based on risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision.
